title: IB French B Common Mistakes and Simple Fixes
summary: IB French B common mistakes can cost easy marks. Learn to read commands, preserve evidence and units, control timing, and improve exam technique.
body_markdown:
**IB French B common mistakes** often involve execution: misreading instructions, selecting incomplete evidence, dropping essential details, using an unsuitable register and losing track of time. Addressing these habits helps you communicate what you already know more accurately.


Imagine Camille, a hypothetical student who understands a passage but answers too quickly. She identifies the right idea without giving the requested evidence, then spends so long polishing her writing that she rushes the final check. Her difficulty illustrates a useful distinction: knowing French and demonstrating that knowledge under exam conditions require practice together.


### Your quick checking routine


Before submitting a response, ask:


- Have I followed the instruction precisely?
- Have I used the required answer format?
- Does my evidence establish the requested point?
- Have I preserved necessary units, dates and qualifiers?
- Does my writing suit its audience, purpose and text type?
- Have I checked for unanswered questions and obvious errors?


Keep this routine short enough to use under pressure. Practise it during ordinary revision so that checking becomes part of answering.


### Misreading the command term


A familiar topic can tempt you to start writing before understanding the task. If a question asks you to justify an answer, identifying the correct idea alone may leave the response incomplete.


Pause before answering. Isolate the instruction, decide what a complete response requires and return to the relevant source. Identification usually calls for a concise detail; justification requires support. A comparison must establish a relationship between the items.


For writing, turn the prompt into a private instruction: “Persuade younger students using a friendly, informed register.” This keeps audience and purpose visible while you plan.


Use the[IB French B Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-french-b/questionbank) to practise interpreting questions alongside understanding French. After each mistake, distinguish a comprehension problem from an instruction problem. The remedy depends on the cause.


### Selecting evidence that does not prove the answer


Locating the right paragraph is only the beginning. A broad quotation may mention the topic without establishing the particular claim in the question.


Choose the smallest passage that provides sufficient evidence. Avoid cutting it so aggressively that you remove a negative, a comparison or another essential qualification. Follow any instruction about quoting or using your own words.


During[French B Paper 2 reading practice](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-french-b/ib-french-b-paper-2-reading) , underline the question’s key idea, locate its equivalent in the text and read your answer against the question. Ask yourself whether someone could understand the connection without guessing.


Listening requires similar attention. Use the available listening opportunities to confirm negatives, quantities and changes of opinion. Expressions such as *ne...plus* , *seulement* and *pourtant* can change the interpretation of an otherwise familiar sentence.


### Losing units and qualifying details


A number can become incomplete when separated from its meaning. If the source says *deux fois par semaine* , writing only *deux fois* loses the frequency. Likewise, *15 euros* and *trois semaines* contain information that the numbers alone cannot communicate.


Capture quantities with their labels. During checking, scan digits and number words specifically, asking whether the response or question supplies enough context. Repeating a unit is unnecessary when the answer field already provides it, but essential information must remain clear.


Use[French B Paper 1 resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-french-b/ib-french-b-paper-1) to practise precise written expression. The[French B self-study guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/best-ib-french-b-resources-self-study) can help you organize separate work on vocabulary, comprehension and exam technique.

### Writing for the wrong audience


Accurate French still needs to fit the situation. A message to a friend and a formal proposal call for different choices in address, tone and organization.


Before drafting, identify the audience, purpose, register and text conventions. Choose a few features that make the communication recognizable, such as an appropriate greeting, headings or a suitable closing. Maintain a consistent form of address throughout.


For example, an invitation should make the occasion and practical details clear while giving the reader a reason to attend. Elaborate vocabulary cannot compensate for missing information.


The guide to[common Language B writing mistakes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-avoid-common-mistakes-in-language-b-writing-expert-tips-and-revisiondojo-resources) supports targeted practice with register and structure. Consult the[French A and B exam structure overview](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-french-a-and-b-exam-structure-explained) for broader assessment context, distinguishing the two courses carefully.


### Spending too long on one response


Timing problems often begin with a reasonable impulse: making one answer better. The cost becomes apparent when later questions receive too little attention.


Divide your available writing or reading time into planning, completion and checking. Set points at which you will move forward. For listening, follow the recording and the instructions rather than applying the same pacing strategy as reading.


Protect a final writing check for agreements, verb forms, accents, register and omitted words. Practise leaving an imperfect sentence temporarily so that one difficulty does not interrupt the whole task.


RevisionDojo’s[Test Builder and Exam Mode](https://www.revisiondojo.com/features/test-builder) can support timed sessions. Review where your pace slipped, alongside which answers were incorrect. The[Mock Exams guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/revisiondojo-mock-exams) offers further preparation context.


### Make each mistake guide your next session


Keep an error log recording the task, mistake, likely cause and next action. Replace “bad listening” with “missed a negative,” then practise identifying negatives in short recordings. Specific diagnoses make revision manageable.


RevisionDojo connects this process across its Questionbank, Study Notes, Flashcards and AI Chat. Grading tools can support response review; Predicted Papers and Mock Exams provide further practice opportunities. Treat predictions as preparation resources rather than promises about exam content. The Coursework Library and Tutors extend support across your wider IB workload.


Use RevisionDojo as your central IB resource: identify one recurring weakness, practise it deliberately and check whether it recurs. The goal is a routine that helps your French knowledge reach the page with clarity and precision.
